# How this homework works (Notes Part 1 & 2, and the assignment's §1.1)

In Part A the truth is *known*, because we generate the data ourselves.
We draw samples from a distribution whose mean and standard deviation we
chose (`rnorm()` for Questions 1–3, `rbinom()` for Question 4), run an
estimator or a test on each sample, repeat that many times, and check how
well the estimator/test recovers the truth we built in. Each question
below therefore has the same three ingredients the assignment asks for:
working code, a plot, and a plain-English interpretation of the results
together with a description of how the code works. `set.seed()` is used
before every simulation (Notes Part 1, §6) so that anyone re-knitting
this file gets exactly the numbers quoted in the text.

---

# Question 1 (15 points) — Three estimators of the standard deviation

**Question in brief.** For sample sizes $n = 2, 3, \dots, 20$, draw
$N = 10{,}000$ samples of each size from a normal distribution with mean
0 and standard deviation 1. For every sample compute three estimators of
the standard deviation: the classical `sd()` (denominator $n-1$ inside
the square root), an alternative with denominator $n$, and an alternative
with denominator $n-2$. For each sample size, summarise each estimator
across the $N$ samples by its mean and its spread (standard deviation),
plot both summaries against $n$, and describe what happens.

**Where this comes from in the notes.** Notes Part 1, §8 defines the two
variance estimators
$S_n^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2$ (called *biased* there) and
$S_{n-1}^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2$ (called *unbiased* there),
and says the difference between estimators matters most for small
samples. This question takes square roots (so we estimate the standard
deviation $\sigma = 1$ itself, not $\sigma^2$) and adds the next
denominator down, $n-2$, as a second "nearest alternative".

## 1.1 The two modified estimators, written as functions

The prompt asks for functions for anything `sd()` does not already do.
Both alternatives are the same sum of squared deviations from the sample
mean, $\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$, divided by a different denominator and
square-rooted. Writing them from the sum (rather than rescaling `sd()`)
keeps the code a direct transcription of the formulas in Notes Part 1, §8.

```{r q1-functions}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# sd.with.n(x): standard-deviation estimator with denominator n.
#   This is sqrt(S_n^2) from Notes Part 1, Eq. (5) — the "biased" estimator:
#   the sample is treated as if it were the whole population.
#   Arguments: x = one numeric sample (a vector of length n).
#   Returns:   one number, the n-denominator estimate of sigma.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
sd.with.n <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)                       # sample size of THIS sample
  sqrt(sum((x - mean(x))^2) / n)       # sum of squared deviations / n, rooted
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# sd.with.n2(x): standard-deviation estimator with denominator n - 2.
#   Same numerator, denominator two smaller than the classical n - 1.
#   EDGE CASE (n = 2): the denominator is 0, so this estimator is UNDEFINED
#   for the smallest sample size in the study. Rather than letting R return
#   Inf (which would poison every mean, spread and plot axis downstream),
#   the function returns NA for n < 3, and every summary below is computed
#   with na.rm = TRUE. The n = 2 row of the results table is therefore
#   blank for this estimator, and its plotted curve starts at n = 3.
#   This is itself part of the answer: an estimator that does not even
#   exist at n = 2 is already at a disadvantage.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
sd.with.n2 <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)                       # sample size of THIS sample
  if (n < 3) return(NA_real_)          # denominator n - 2 would be <= 0
  sqrt(sum((x - mean(x))^2) / (n - 2)) # sum of squared deviations / (n-2)
}
```

## 1.2 The simulation loop (following the scaffold given in the prompt)

The scaffold in the assignment fixes the object names and the structure:
`max.sample.size`, `n.sim`, one results matrix per estimator
(`sd.ori`, `sd.n`, `sd.n.2`), and a double loop over sample sizes and
re-samplings. Two disclosed changes from the printed scaffold, both
purely mechanical: (i) the matrices are initialised with `NA` instead of
`0`, so that the never-used first column (sample sizes start at 2, so
column 1 is never written) and the undefined $n-2$ values at $n=2$ do
not enter the summaries as fake zeros; (ii) each iteration draws the
sample **once** into `x` and computes all three estimators on that same
sample, exactly as the scaffold's comments require ("for the same
sample") — drawing three separate samples would compare estimators on
different data and defeat the purpose.

```{r q1-simulation}
#### Set up looping numbers ####
##################################
max.sample.size <- 20
n.sim <- 10000  # number of re-samplings we are going to run for each sample size

#### Set up matrices to save data. ####
# Rows    = one row per re-sampling (n.sim rows).
# Columns = one column per sample size; column j holds the results for
#           samples of size j, so columns 2..20 are used and column 1
#           simply stays NA (there is no sample of size 1 in this study).
sd.ori <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n.sim, ncol = max.sample.size) # classical sd, n-1
sd.n   <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n.sim, ncol = max.sample.size) # alternative, n
sd.n.2 <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n.sim, ncol = max.sample.size) # alternative, n-2

set.seed(111)  # reproducible "random" numbers (Notes Part 1, Section 6)

#### Perform computations in a loop ####
########################################
for (sample.size in 2:max.sample.size) {      # outer loop: sample size n
  for (i.sim in 1:n.sim) {                    # inner loop: re-sampling number
    # Draw ONE new random sample of size sample.size from the normal
    # distribution with mean 0 and sd 1 — the known truth is sigma = 1.
    x <- rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1)

    # (a) The "classical" sd of this sample (denominator n - 1, built-in sd()).
    x.sd <- sd(x)
    sd.ori[i.sim, sample.size] <- x.sd        # save it where it belongs in sd.ori

    # (b) The first modified estimator (denominator n), SAME sample x.
    sd.n[i.sim, sample.size] <- sd.with.n(x)  # save it where it belongs in sd.n

    # (c) The second modified estimator (denominator n - 2), SAME sample x.
    #     Returns NA when sample.size == 2 (see the function's edge case).
    sd.n.2[i.sim, sample.size] <- sd.with.n2(x)
  }
}
```

## 1.3 Summarising each estimator: mean and spread at each sample size

Each column of a results matrix holds $N = 10{,}000$ values of one
estimator at one sample size — i.e. 10,000 realisations of that estimator
as a *random variable* (Notes Part 1, §8: an estimator is computed from a
random sample, so it is itself random). `apply(..., 2, ...)` runs a
summary function down each column, the same use of `apply()` as in
Week2 Script.R, Part 2, Code Chunk 5.

```{r q1-summaries}
# The sample sizes actually studied, used as row labels / plot x-values.
sizes <- 2:max.sample.size

# MEAN of each estimator across the 10,000 re-samplings, per sample size.
# If an estimator is "aimed at" sigma = 1, its mean should sit at 1.
mean.ori <- apply(sd.ori[, sizes], 2, mean)                  # classical, n-1
mean.n   <- apply(sd.n[,   sizes], 2, mean)                  # alternative, n
mean.n2  <- apply(sd.n.2[, sizes], 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE)    # alternative, n-2
mean.n2[is.nan(mean.n2)] <- NA_real_  # n = 2 column is entirely NA (estimator
                                      # undefined there); display NA, not NaN

# SPREAD (standard deviation) of each estimator across the re-samplings.
# This measures precision: how much the estimate wobbles from sample to
# sample of the same size. Smaller spread = more trustworthy single estimate.
spread.ori <- apply(sd.ori[, sizes], 2, sd)                  # classical, n-1
spread.n   <- apply(sd.n[,   sizes], 2, sd)                  # alternative, n
spread.n2  <- apply(sd.n.2[, sizes], 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)    # alternative, n-2

# Put the summaries in one table so the numbers behind the plots are visible.
q1.table <- data.frame(
  n            = sizes,
  mean_s       = round(mean.ori, 3),   # mean of classical estimator
  mean_s_n     = round(mean.n,   3),   # mean of n-denominator estimator
  mean_s_n2    = round(mean.n2,  3),   # mean of (n-2)-denominator estimator
  spread_s     = round(spread.ori, 3), # spread of classical estimator
  spread_s_n   = round(spread.n,   3), # spread of n-denominator estimator
  spread_s_n2  = round(spread.n2,  3)  # spread of (n-2)-denominator estimator
)
q1.table
```

## 1.4 Plots: means and spreads against sample size

Following the hint in the prompt, each panel is first opened as a blank
plot of the right size with `plot(..., type = "n")`, and the three
estimators are then added one series at a time with `points()`.

```{r q1-plot-means}
# ---- Panel 1: MEAN of each estimator vs. sample size ----------------------
# Blank plot sized to fit all three series (ylim is set from ALL three
# means: the n-2 series rises above 1 at small n and would be clipped by
# an axis sized on the classical series alone). The dashed line marks
# the truth, sigma = 1, that every estimator is trying to recover.
plot(sizes, mean.ori, type = "n",
     ylim = c(0.5, max(mean.n2, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Sample size n", ylab = "Mean of the sd estimates (10,000 samples)",
     main = "Q1: Average sd estimate vs. sample size (true sigma = 1)")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")            # the true value, sigma = 1
points(sizes, mean.ori, pch = 19, col = "black")  # classical s (n - 1)
points(sizes, mean.n,   pch = 17, col = "red")    # s with denominator n
points(sizes, mean.n2,  pch = 15, col = "blue")   # s with denominator n - 2
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("s  (denominator n - 1)", "s_n  (denominator n)",
                  "s_n-2  (denominator n - 2)", "true sigma = 1"),
       pch = c(19, 17, 15, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 2),
       col = c("black", "red", "blue", "grey40"))
```

```{r q1-plot-spreads}
# ---- Panel 2: SPREAD of each estimator vs. sample size --------------------
# Same construction: blank plot first (ylim again sized on all three
# series, since the n-2 estimator wobbles most), then one points()
# series per estimator. There is no single "true" spread to mark — the
# question here is how fast each estimator's wobble shrinks as n grows,
# and which wobbles most.
plot(sizes, spread.ori, type = "n",
     ylim = c(0, max(spread.n2, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Sample size n", ylab = "SD of the sd estimates (10,000 samples)",
     main = "Q1: Spread (precision) of the sd estimates vs. sample size")
points(sizes, spread.ori, pch = 19, col = "black")  # classical s (n - 1)
points(sizes, spread.n,   pch = 17, col = "red")    # s with denominator n
points(sizes, spread.n2,  pch = 15, col = "blue")   # s with denominator n - 2
legend("topright",
       legend = c("s  (denominator n - 1)", "s_n  (denominator n)",
                  "s_n-2  (denominator n - 2)"),
       pch = c(19, 17, 15), col = c("black", "red", "blue"))
```

## 1.5 Interpretation (plain English)

**How to read the two panels.** The first panel is about *aim*: averaged
over 10,000 samples of the same size, does the estimator land on the true
value $\sigma = 1$? The second panel is about *steadiness*: how widely
individual estimates scatter around their own average.

**What the simulation shows.**

* **The $n$-denominator estimator ($s_n$, red) aims too low.** Dividing
  the same sum of squares by a *larger* denominator can only make the
  result smaller, and at small $n$ the shortfall is large: at $n = 2$ its
  mean is only about `r round(mean.n[1], 2)` instead of 1, and it is
  still visibly below 1 at $n = 5$ (about `r round(mean.n[4], 2)`). This
  is exactly the bias the notes attribute to $S_n^2$ in Notes Part 1, §8:
  the sample mean $\bar x$ is computed from the same data, so deviations
  from $\bar x$ are on average a little smaller than deviations from the
  true mean, and dividing by $n$ does nothing to compensate. This is a
  *systematic* error — collecting more samples of the same small size
  would not fix it, because the average itself is in the wrong place.
* **The $(n-2)$-denominator estimator ($s_{n-2}$, blue) over-corrects.**
  Dividing by a *smaller* denominator inflates every estimate: its mean
  sits *above* 1 (about `r round(mean.n2[2], 2)` at $n = 3$, the smallest
  size where it exists at all), and it is not even defined at $n = 2$,
  where the denominator is 0. It also has the *largest spread* of the
  three at every small sample size (panel 2) — the inflation factor
  $\sqrt{(n-1)/(n-2)}$ multiplies the whole estimate, wobble included.
  So this alternative is both aimed too high and the least steady.
* **The classical $s$ (denominator $n-1$, black) is aimed best, but is
  not perfect either.** Its mean is the closest of the three to 1 at
  every sample size, yet it still sits slightly *below* 1 for small $n$
  (about `r round(mean.ori[1], 2)` at $n = 2`). That small remaining dip
  is a square-root effect, not a failure of the $n-1$ correction: $n-1$
  makes the *variance* estimator $S_{n-1}^2$ unbiased, but taking the
  square root of an unbiased estimator does not give an unbiased
  estimator of the square root — averaging square roots of quantities
  that scatter symmetrically around $\sigma^2$ lands a little below
  $\sigma$. The simulation makes this subtlety visible, which an
  algebraic look at the variance formula alone would hide.
* **All three estimators converge as $n$ grows.** By $n = 20$ the three
  means are about `r round(mean.ori[length(sizes)], 3)` (classical),
  `r round(mean.n[length(sizes)], 3)` ($n$) and
  `r round(mean.n2[length(sizes)], 3)` ($n-2$) — nearly indistinguishable,
  because $n$, $n-1$ and $n-2$ are nearly the same number when $n$ is 20.
  The notes make the same point in words ("the difference between the
  two estimators becomes negligible as $n$ increases", Part 1, §8); the
  plot is that sentence, quantified.
* **Spread shrinks for everyone, in the same order at every $n$.** At
  $n = 2$ a single classical estimate has spread about
  `r round(spread.ori[1], 2)` — an estimate of $\sigma = 1$ from two
  observations can easily come out at 0.3 or 1.6 — while by $n = 20$ the
  spread is down to about `r round(spread.ori[length(sizes)], 2)`. The
  ordering never changes: $s_n$ is marginally the steadiest (dividing by
  the larger $n$ shrinks the wobble along with the estimate itself —
  steady but aimed at the wrong value), $s$ is next, and $s_{n-2}$ is
  always the wobbliest.

**Bottom line.** The denominator is a bias–precision trade-off that only
matters at small $n$. Of the three, the classical $n-1$ estimator is the
right default: nearly on target at all sizes shown and almost as steady
as the steadiest alternative, while $s_n$ is systematically too small
and $s_{n-2}$ is systematically too large, less steady, and undefined at
$n = 2$.

# Question 2 (28 points) — The t-test under the null, by simulation

**Question in brief.** Draw two samples of different sizes from the
*same* normal distribution, compute the difference between their means
and the p-value of a t-test on the same two samples, and repeat
$N = 10^4$ times. From the $N$ simulated differences, compute a
brute-force p-value for each difference from its rank among all $N$
differences. Make the six requested plots (a)–(f). Then repeat the whole
study with sample sizes four times larger and explain how the agreement
between the simulated (brute-force) and calculated (t-test) p-values
changes, and why.

**Where this comes from in the notes.** This is the ALL-ages experiment
of Notes Part 2, §2 run on simulated instead of real data: there, two
samples were re-drawn from one common distribution 10,000 times, the
difference of means was recorded each time, and the brute-force answer
(the fraction of re-draws at least as extreme as the original, about
0.119) was compared with the t-test's answer (about 0.123). §3 then
names the pieces: the *null hypothesis* (here: both samples come from
distributions with the same mean), the *test statistic* (here: the
difference between the sample means), and the *p-value* (the probability,
under the null, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one
observed).

**Choices made, and consistency between the two methods (the hint).**
The distribution is normal with mean $\mu = 2$ and variance
$\sigma^2 = 3$, i.e. `sd = sqrt(3)`, the example values named in the
prompt. Both samples in every pair are drawn from this *same*
distribution, so the null hypothesis is *true by construction* — any
non-zero difference of means is pure sampling fluctuation. I use
**two-sided** tests throughout: the t-test is run with its default
two-sided alternative, and the brute-force p-value is therefore built
from the *absolute* difference (Step 4 of the prompt's outline: rank of
the negative absolute value), so the two p-values answer exactly the
same question — "how often would a difference *this far from zero in
either direction* occur under the null?". Mixing a one-sided rank with
a two-sided t-test would manufacture a spurious factor-of-two
disagreement.

## 2.1 One pair of samples, worked once by hand

Before the mass simulation, one single experiment, exactly as the first
bullet of the question asks:

```{r q2-single-pair}
set.seed(222)  # reproducible draws (Notes Part 1, Section 6)

# The one common underlying distribution: mean 2, variance 3.
mu.true    <- 2
sigma.true <- sqrt(3)   # variance = 3  =>  sd = sqrt(3)

# First sample sizes, as suggested in the prompt.
n1 <- 5
n2 <- 7

# Draw the two samples from the SAME distribution (null is true).
x1 <- rnorm(n1, mean = mu.true, sd = sigma.true)  # sample 1, size n1
x2 <- rnorm(n2, mean = mu.true, sd = sigma.true)  # sample 2, size n2
x1
x2

# Difference between the samples' means — the test statistic.
mean.diff.single <- mean(x1) - mean(x2)
mean.diff.single

# p-value of a (two-sided, default) t-test run on the same two samples.
# t.test() returns a list; $p.value is the element we need — the same
# access pattern as t.test(...)$p.value in Notes Part 2, Section 2 and
# in Week2 Script.R, Part 2, Code Chunks 4-5.
t.test(x1, x2)$p.value
```

Neither number means anything on its own: a difference of this size, and
a p-value like this, are exactly what the null produces routinely. The
rest of the question asks *how routinely*, by repeating the experiment
10,000 times.

## 2.2 The resampling study, wrapped in one function

Following the prompt's outline and its advice to wrap the whole study in
a function (so the larger-sample run is a single new call, with no code
rewritten):

* **Step 1** — build one matrix holding all the resamplings:
  10,000 rows, $n_1 + n_2$ columns (12 columns for $n_1=5, n_2=7$).
  Each row is one complete experiment: the first $n_1$ entries are
  "sample 1", the remaining $n_2$ entries are "sample 2".
* **Step 2** — define `mean.diff()`, the difference of the two sample
  means within one row, using the outline's indexing
  `x[1:n1]` and `x[(n1+1):(n1+n2)]`.
* **Step 3** — apply `mean.diff()` to every row (`apply(..., 1, ...)`,
  the row-wise use of `apply()`), giving the vector of 10,000
  differences; also apply a t-test to every row and keep its p-value.
* **Step 4** — brute-force p-value of each difference from its rank:
  `rank(-abs(diff)) / N`. Ranking the *negative absolute* difference
  puts the largest $|\text{difference}|$ first (rank 1), so a difference
  that is the 2nd most extreme of 10,000 gets p $= 2/10000$ — the
  prompt's own one-sided example, with the absolute value making it the
  two-sided version that matches the t-test used here.

```{r q2-function}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# resample.study(n1, n2, n.sim, mu, sigma, seed)
#   Runs one complete Question-2 study at sample sizes n1 and n2.
#   Returns a list with the simulated differences of means (diff),
#   the t-test p-value for each resampling (t.p), the brute-force
#   p-value for each resampling (brute.p), and the sizes used.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
resample.study <- function(n1, n2, n.sim = 10000,
                           mu = 2, sigma = sqrt(3), seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)  # each study is reproducible on its own

  ## Step 1: the resampling matrix — n.sim rows x (n1 + n2) columns.
  ## Every entry is an independent draw from the SAME normal
  ## distribution, so in every row both "samples" obey the null.
  sim.mat <- matrix(rnorm(n.sim * (n1 + n2), mean = mu, sd = sigma),
                    nrow = n.sim, ncol = n1 + n2) }

#   ## Step 2: difference between the means of sample 1 and sample 2
#   ## within one row x of the matrix (indexing as in the prompt outline).
#   mean.diff <- function(x) mean(x[1:n1]) - mean(x[(n1 + 1):(n1 + n2)])
# 
#   ## Step 3a: the difference in means for all rows of the matrix.
#   diff.sim <- apply(sim.mat, 1, mean.diff)
# 
#   ## Step 3b: the t-test p-value for all rows of the matrix.
#   ## A small local function runs the two-sided t-test on one row and
#   ## keeps only its p-value; apply() runs it on every row.
#   t.p.row <- function(x) t.test(x[1:n1], x[(n1 + 1):(n1 + n2)])$p.value
#   t.p.sim <- apply(sim.mat, 1, t.p.row)
# 
#   ## Step 4: the brute-force p-value of each difference, from its rank.
#   ## rank(-abs(diff)) is small exactly when |diff| is large (extreme);
#   ## dividing by the number of resamplings turns the rank into the
#   ## fraction of resamplings at least as extreme — a p-value obtained
#   ## without any t-distribution mathematics at all.
#   brute.p.sim <- rank(-abs(diff.sim)) / n.sim
# 
#   ## Hand everything back in one list.
#   list(n1 = n1, n2 = n2, diff = diff.sim,
#        t.p = t.p.sim, brute.p = brute.p.sim)
# }

# Run 1: the original small sample sizes, n1 = 5 and n2 = 7.
study.small <- resample.study(n1 = 5, n2 = 7, seed = 202)

# A few summary numbers for the small-sample study, used in the text:
# the centre and spread of the simulated differences, the fraction of
# t-tests that (incorrectly-looking) come out "significant" at 0.05,
# and two agreement measures between the two kinds of p-value.
summary.small <- c(
  mean.diff      = mean(study.small$diff),                 # should be ~ 0
  sd.diff        = sd(study.small$diff),                   # spread of diffs
  frac.t.sig     = mean(study.small$t.p < 0.05),           # should be ~ 0.05
  frac.brute.sig = mean(study.small$brute.p < 0.05),       # should be ~ 0.05
  cor.p          = cor(study.small$t.p, study.small$brute.p),
  mean.abs.diff.p = mean(abs(study.small$t.p - study.small$brute.p))
)
round(summary.small, 4)
```

## 2.3 The six requested plots — small samples ($n_1 = 5$, $n_2 = 7$)

One plotting function draws all six panels for any study, so the
large-sample run below produces the identical figure for comparison.
`par(mfrow = c(2, 3))` lays the six panels out in one figure, the same
`par()` device-splitting used in Notes Part 2, §2.

```{r q2-plot-function}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# plot.study(study, label): draws panels (a)-(f) of the question for one
#   resample.study() result. study = the list returned by resample.study();
#   label = text identifying the sample sizes, used in the figure title.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
plot.study <- function(study, label) {
  old.par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3))  # 6 panels in one figure; restore after
  on.exit(par(old.par))

  # (a) Distribution of the differences observed in all the resamplings.
  hist(study$diff, breaks = 40,
       xlab = "Difference between the sample means",
       main = "(a) Differences of means")
  abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")  # differences centre on the null value 0

  # (b) Distribution of the t-test p-values from each resampling.
  hist(study$t.p, breaks = 20, xlim = c(0, 1),
       xlab = "t-test p-value", main = "(b) t-test p-values")

  # (c) Distribution of the brute-force p-values from each resampling.
  hist(study$brute.p, breaks = 20, xlim = c(0, 1),
       xlab = "Brute-force p-value", main = "(c) Brute-force p-values")

  # (d) t-test p-value versus the difference between the means:
  #     one point per resampling experiment.
  plot(study$diff, study$t.p, pch = ".",
       xlab = "Difference between the sample means", ylab = "t-test p-value",
       main = "(d) t-test p vs. difference")

  # (e) Brute-force p-value versus the difference between the means:
  #     x-axis = difference, y-axis = p-value, one point per experiment.
  plot(study$diff, study$brute.p, pch = ".",
       xlab = "Difference between the sample means",
       ylab = "Brute-force p-value",
       main = "(e) Brute-force p vs. difference")

  # (f) t-test p-values vs. brute-force p-values.
  #     The dashed line is y = x: perfect agreement between the methods.
  plot(study$brute.p, study$t.p, pch = ".",
       xlab = "Brute-force p-value", ylab = "t-test p-value",
       main = "(f) t-test p vs. brute-force p")
  abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
}
```

```{r q2-plots-small, fig.height=7}
plot.study(study.small, "n1 = 5, n2 = 7")
```

## 2.4 Repeat with sample sizes four times larger ($n_1 = 20$, $n_2 = 28$)

No new code — the function from §2.2 is simply called again with the new
parameters, as the prompt suggests:

```{r q2-large, fig.height=7}
# Run 2: sample sizes multiplied by 4 (5 -> 20 and 7 -> 28).
study.large <- resample.study(n1 = 20, n2 = 28, seed = 203)

summary.large <- c(
  mean.diff      = mean(study.large$diff),
  sd.diff        = sd(study.large$diff),
  frac.t.sig     = mean(study.large$t.p < 0.05),
  frac.brute.sig = mean(study.large$brute.p < 0.05),
  cor.p          = cor(study.large$t.p, study.large$brute.p),
  mean.abs.diff.p = mean(abs(study.large$t.p - study.large$brute.p))
)
round(summary.large, 4)

plot.study(study.large, "n1 = 20, n2 = 28")
```

## 2.5 Interpretation (plain English)

**Panel (a) — the differences.** The 10,000 differences form a smooth,
symmetric, bell-shaped cloud centred on 0 (mean
`r round(mean(study.small$diff), 3)` in the small study). That is the
null hypothesis drawn as a picture: when both samples really do come
from the same distribution, the difference of their means is a random
variable centred exactly on "no difference", and a difference of, say,
$\pm 1$ is unremarkable while $\pm 3$ is rare. The spread of this cloud
is the yardstick for everything else — a difference is "extreme" only
relative to how wide this cloud is.

**Panels (b) and (c) — both sets of p-values are flat.** Under a true
null, p-values should be *uniform* on $[0,1]$: a p-value is the
probability of something at least as extreme, so 5% of experiments
should land below 0.05, 5% between 0.05 and 0.10, and so on. Both
histograms look flat, and the counts agree: the t-test calls
`r round(100 * mean(study.small$t.p < 0.05), 1)`% of these null
experiments "significant" at 0.05, and the brute-force method calls
`r round(100 * mean(study.small$brute.p < 0.05), 1)`% significant. In
other words, both methods "cry wolf" at exactly the advertised rate
when there is no wolf — which is all a p-value ever promises.

**Panels (d) and (e) — same shape, different smoothness.** In both
panels, small $|\text{difference}|$ (centre) goes with large p-values
and large $|\text{difference}|$ (both tails) goes with p-values near 0:
extremeness and p-value are two descriptions of the same thing. The
brute-force panel (e) is a perfectly clean curve, because the
brute-force p-value is a *deterministic function of the difference
alone* — it is nothing but the difference's rank, so every point lies
exactly on one curve. The t-test panel (d), by contrast, is a fuzzy
band: two experiments with the *same* difference of means can get quite
different t-test p-values. The reason is inside the t-statistic
(Notes Part 2, §3.1): the t-test does not judge the difference by the
true $\sigma$ (which the brute-force cloud effectively uses, because it
is built from 10,000 realisations) but by the *sample* standard
deviations of that particular pair of samples,
$T = (\bar X_1 - \bar X_2)\,/\,\text{(spread estimated from these two
samples)}$. If a pair of samples happens to have unusually small sample
variances, the same difference looks more significant; if the samples
happen to be extra spread out, it looks less significant. The
brute-force method has no such per-experiment noise.

**Panel (f) — the two methods agree, imperfectly at small $n$.** The
points cluster around the $y = x$ line (correlation
`r round(cor(study.small$t.p, study.small$brute.p), 3)`, average
absolute disagreement
`r round(mean(abs(study.small$t.p - study.small$brute.p)), 3)`), so the
fast analytical t-test and the slow brute-force resampling are
essentially answering the same question — the same conclusion the notes
drew from a single comparison (0.119 brute-force vs. 0.123 t-test) in
Notes Part 2, §2, now confirmed across all 10,000 experiments at once.
But the cloud around the line is visibly thick at $n_1=5, n_2=7$: for
any individual small-sample experiment, the t-test p-value can be
appreciably above or below the brute-force value.

**What changes at four times the sample size, and why.** Three things
improve together in the $n_1=20, n_2=28$ run. (1) The differences cloud
narrows — its standard deviation falls from
`r round(sd(study.small$diff), 2)` to
`r round(sd(study.large$diff), 2)`, close to the factor of 2 expected
from quadrupling $n$ (spread of a mean shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$) — so
chance differences are simply smaller. (2) Panel (d)'s fuzzy band
tightens toward panel (e)'s clean curve. (3) Panel (f)'s cloud hugs the
$y=x$ line more closely: the correlation rises to
`r round(cor(study.large$t.p, study.large$brute.p), 3)` and the average
absolute disagreement between the two p-values falls to
`r round(mean(abs(study.large$t.p - study.large$brute.p)), 3)`. The
mechanism is the one the question points at: the t-test's only
approximation is its *variance estimate*. Each sample variance is itself
a random variable (Question 1 was entirely about such estimators!), and
with 20–28 observations per sample it is estimated far more precisely
than with 5–7, so the denominator of the t-statistic is nearly the same
in every experiment and nearly equal to the true spread that the
brute-force distribution embodies. With the denominator stabilised, the
t-test p-value becomes almost a function of the difference alone —
which is exactly what the brute-force p-value is — and the two methods
converge. The brute-force method, notably, does not change its
character at all: its p-values are ranks by construction at any sample
size, which is why this same logic can be reused on real data in
Question 5, where no t-distribution assumption is available.

# Question 3 (18 points) — A non-significant t-test between two very different processes

**Question in brief.** Using `rnorm()`, create two samples that produce
an *insignificant* t-test p-value yet come from two very different
processes. (Hint from the prompt: if one sample comes from a standard
normal, mean 0 and sd 1, and the other from the union of two normals
with means mirrored on either side of zero, e.g. $-10$ and $+10$, both
distributions have mean 0.) Plot the two distributions, then repeat the
sampling many times, collect the t-test p-value each time, and plot and
discuss the distribution of those p-values.

**The construction.** Process A is the standard normal,
$N(0, 1)$. Process B is a *mixture*: each observation is drawn from
$N(-10, 1)$ or from $N(+10, 1)$ with equal chance. B's distribution is
two separated spikes with a gap in the middle — nothing like a single
bell curve — and its standard deviation is about
$\sqrt{10^2 + 1} \approx 10$, ten times A's. But the two spikes are
symmetric around 0, so B's mean is exactly 0, the same as A's. A
function keeps the recipe in one place so the plot and the repeated
trials below use identical processes:

```{r q3-generator}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# draw.mixture(n): draws n values from Process B, the "union" (mixture)
#   of N(-10, 1) and N(+10, 1). EACH observation independently belongs
#   to one component or the other with equal chance: sample() picks a
#   centre, -10 or +10, separately for every draw (the same sample()
#   used for resampling in Notes Part 2, Section 2), and rnorm() then
#   draws around the chosen centres. Because the components are mirror
#   images around 0, the mixture's true mean is 0 while its true sd is
#   about sqrt(10^2 + 1) = 10.05.
#   Why per-draw choice matters: fixing exactly half the draws in each
#   component would force every sample's mean to almost the same value
#   and rig the experiment in 3(b) — the random fluctuation of the
#   mixture sample's mean (sometimes more +10s than -10s, sometimes
#   fewer) is precisely what the repeated t-tests below are studying.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
draw.mixture <- function(n) {
  centres <- sample(c(-10, 10), size = n, replace = TRUE) # one coin flip per draw
  rnorm(n, mean = centres, sd = 1)  # draw around each chosen centre
}
```

## 3(a) The two distributions, plotted

Large samples (1,000 values each) are drawn once so the *shapes* of the
two distributions — not small-sample noise — are what the histograms
show:

```{r q3-plot-distributions}
set.seed(333)  # reproducible draws (Notes Part 1, Section 6)

# One large sample from each process, to display the distributions.
big.normal  <- rnorm(1000, mean = 0, sd = 1)  # Process A: standard normal
big.mixture <- draw.mixture(1000)             # Process B: two-spike mixture

# Side-by-side histograms. NOTE the x-axes: they are deliberately left
# at each sample's own range so both shapes are visible; Process B's
# axis runs roughly -14 to +14, Process A's only -4 to +4.
old.par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(big.normal, breaks = 30,
     xlab = "Value", main = "Process A: N(0, 1)")
hist(big.mixture, breaks = 30,
     xlab = "Value", main = "Process B: union of N(-10, 1) and N(+10, 1)")
par(old.par)

# The numerical summaries tell the same story as the pictures:
# means (nearly) identical, standard deviations ten-fold apart.
c(mean.A = mean(big.normal),  sd.A = sd(big.normal),
  mean.B = mean(big.mixture), sd.B = sd(big.mixture))
```

The two processes could hardly be more different: A is a single hump
concentrated between $-3$ and $+3$; B has *no* values near its own mean
at all — a value of 0, the centre of both distributions, is routine
under A and essentially impossible under B — and B's values spread ten
times wider. A single illustrative pair of moderate-sized samples shows
the t-test's reaction to all of this difference:

```{r q3-single-pair}
set.seed(334)

# One pair of samples of the size used in the repeated trials below.
n3 <- 25
sample.A <- rnorm(n3, mean = 0, sd = 1)  # 25 draws from Process A
sample.B <- draw.mixture(n3)             # 25 draws from Process B

# t-test of the two samples (two-sided, default settings, as throughout).
t.test(sample.A, sample.B)$p.value
```

With this seed the p-value is
`r round(t.test(sample.A, sample.B)$p.value, 3)` — nowhere near
significant — even though the two samples were generated by completely
different mechanisms.

## 3(b) The t-test p-value, repeated many times

One non-significant result could be luck. The question therefore asks
for the whole distribution of p-values over repeated trials:

```{r q3-repeated}
set.seed(335)

n.trials <- 1000   # number of repeated experiments
p.q3 <- numeric(n.trials)  # empty vector to hold one p-value per trial

# Each trial: draw a FRESH sample from each process (same sizes as the
# illustrative pair above) and record the t-test p-value.
for (i in 1:n.trials) {
  a <- rnorm(n3, mean = 0, sd = 1)  # fresh sample from Process A
  b <- draw.mixture(n3)             # fresh sample from Process B
  p.q3[i] <- t.test(a, b)$p.value   # keep only the p-value
}

# Histogram of the 1,000 p-values, with the conventional 0.05 cutoff marked.
hist(p.q3, breaks = 20, xlim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "t-test p-value", main = "Q3: t-test p-values, A vs. B (1,000 trials)")
abline(v = 0.05, lty = 2, col = "red")

# Fraction of trials that DO come out "significant" at 0.05.
mean(p.q3 < 0.05)
```

## 3(c) Interpretation (plain English)

The histogram is approximately *flat* over $[0, 1]$, and only about
`r round(100 * mean(p.q3 < 0.05), 1)`% of the 1,000 trials are
significant at 0.05 — statistically indistinguishable from what
Question 2 produced when the two samples came from *literally the same*
distribution. That is not a bug in the simulation; it is the t-test
working exactly as defined, and it exposes precisely what the t-test
does and does not test.

The two-sample t-test's null hypothesis (Notes Part 2, §3–3.1) is a
statement about **means only**: "the two underlying distributions have
the same mean". Its test statistic is the difference between the sample
means, rescaled by the samples' spread. By symmetry, both of our
processes have mean exactly 0, so *the null hypothesis of the t-test is
true here* — even though the distributions are wildly different in
shape and spread. A test that is asked only "are the means equal?" and
is told the truth "yes" answers with uniformly distributed p-values,
exactly as in Question 2. The roughly 5% of trials that come out
significant are the test's ordinary false-alarm rate: in those trials,
chance put a few more $+10$ than $-10$ draws (or vice versa) into the
small mixture sample, nudging its sample mean away from 0.

Two practical lessons follow. First, **"not significant" does not mean
"the same"**: a non-significant t-test rules out (at the chosen level)
a difference *in means*; it says nothing whatsoever about variance,
shape, bimodality, or mechanism. Reporting only the t-test for these
two samples would describe two utterly different biological processes
as indistinguishable. Second, the difference between the processes here
*is* easily detectable — just not by a test of means: the sample
standard deviations differ ten-fold in every trial
(`r round(sd(big.normal), 2)` vs. `r round(sd(big.mixture), 2)` in the
large samples above), and the histograms in part (a) are visibly
unlike. Choosing a test means choosing which aspect of "different" you
are asking about; the t-test's aspect is the mean, and only the mean.

# Question 4 (15 points) — A counting question: the binomial distribution

**Question in brief.** A diagnostic test has sensitivity 0.8 — each
truly positive patient is detected with probability $p = 0.8$,
independently of the others (a Bernoulli trial per patient, in the
language of Notes Part 1, §3 and §5). We screen $n = 15$ patients who
are all truly positive, and let $X$ be the number who test positive, so
$X$ is binomial with $n = 15$, $p = 0.8$. Find the probability of
exactly 10 positives by hand, confirm it with `dbinom()`, find the
probability of at least 10 positives two analytic ways, confirm it a
third way by simulation with `rbinom()`, and use `qbinom()` to find
the smallest count $k$ with $P(X \ge k) \le 0.05$.

The one formula needed is the binomial probability from Notes Part 1,
§5:

$$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}\, p^{k}\, (1-p)^{\,n-k},
\qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} = \texttt{choose(n, k) in R}.$$

```{r q4-setup}
# Fixed quantities for the whole question.
n.patients <- 15   # n: patients screened, all truly positive
p.sens     <- 0.8  # p: sensitivity = P(one truly positive patient tests +)
```

## 4(a) By hand: the probability of exactly 10 positives

**By hand.** With $n = 15$, $k = 10$, $p = 0.8$:

1. *Choose which patients.* The 10 detected patients can be any 10 of
   the 15: $\binom{15}{10} = \frac{15!}{10!\,5!} =
   \frac{15 \cdot 14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12 \cdot 11}{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3
   \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \frac{360360}{120} = 3003$ different sets.
2. *Probability of one such pattern.* Any one specific pattern with 10
   detections and 5 misses has probability
   $0.8^{10} \times 0.2^{5}$ (the trials are independent, so the
   per-patient probabilities multiply — Notes Part 1, §5).
   Numerically, $0.8^{10} = 0.107374$ and $0.2^{5} = 0.00032$, so one
   pattern has probability $0.107374 \times 0.00032 = 0.0000344$
   (about $3.4 \times 10^{-5}$).
3. *Add the patterns.* All 3003 patterns have the same probability and
   are mutually exclusive, so
   $P(X = 10) = 3003 \times 0.8^{10} \times 0.2^{5}
   = 3003 \times 0.0000344 \approx 0.1032$.

So even though 12 positives is the *expected* count ($15 \times 0.8$),
getting *exactly* 10 is about a 10% event. The chunk below repeats
exactly these three steps in code — the same
`choose(15, k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k)` expression the notes use to plot a
binomial distribution by hand (Notes Part 1, §5; Week2 Script.R,
Part 1, Code Chunk 3):

```{r q4a-hand}
# Step 1: the binomial coefficient, by the choose() function of the notes
# and, to show the work, by the factorial definition directly.
choose(15, 10)                                  # = 3003
factorial(15) / (factorial(10) * factorial(5))  # same number, by hand

# Steps 2-3: one pattern's probability, times the number of patterns.
choose(15, 10) * 0.8^10 * 0.2^5                 # = 0.1032 (see 4b)
```

## 4(b) Confirmation with `dbinom()`

`dbinom(k, n, p)` is the "d" member of the binomial's d/p/q/r family
(Notes Part 1, §6): it evaluates the same formula directly.

```{r q4b-dbinom}
dbinom(10, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)  # P(X = 10), from dbinom()
# Compare with the hand result from 4(a): the two agree.
choose(15, 10) * 0.8^10 * 0.2^5 - dbinom(10, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)
```

## 4(c) The probability of at least 10 positives, two analytic ways

"At least 10" is the event $X \ge 10$, i.e. $X \in \{10, 11, 12, 13, 14,
15\}$. **Way 1 — `pbinom()`:** `pbinom(q, n, p)` is the cumulative
$P(X \le q)$, so $P(X \ge 10) = 1 - P(X \le 9)$ — the complement is
taken at **9**, not 10, because 10 itself belongs to the event we want
(the standard off-by-one trap with discrete distributions).
**Way 2 — summing `dbinom()`:** add the six individual probabilities.

```{r q4c-atleast}
# Way 1: the CDF (pbinom) and the complement rule.
p.atleast.pbinom <- 1 - pbinom(9, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)
p.atleast.pbinom

# Way 2: sum the individual dbinom() probabilities for 10 through 15.
p.atleast.sum <- sum(dbinom(10:15, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens))
p.atleast.sum

# The two approaches agree (difference is zero up to rounding).
p.atleast.pbinom - p.atleast.sum
```

Both give $P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.9389$: with a test this sensitive and
15 truly positive patients, at least 10 detections is the overwhelming
norm, not a lucky outcome.

## 4(d) The same answer a third way: simulation with `rbinom()`

`rbinom(N, n, p)` draws $N$ independent binomial counts — $N$ simulated
repeats of the whole 15-patient screen. The fraction of repeats with at
least 10 positives should land close to the analytic 0.9389, by the
same "simulate it, then check it against the theoretical answer" logic
as Questions 1 and 2 (and the error should be of order
$\sqrt{0.94 \times 0.06 / 10000} \approx 0.002$):

```{r q4d-simulation}
set.seed(444)  # reproducible draws (Notes Part 1, Section 6)

# 10,000 simulated screens of 15 patients each.
sim.q4 <- rbinom(10000, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)

# Simulated P(X >= 10): the proportion of screens with >= 10 positives.
mean(sim.q4 >= 10)

# For completeness, the simulated P(X = 10) as well, against part (a)/(b).
mean(sim.q4 == 10)

# Side by side with the analytic answers:
c(simulated.at.least.10 = mean(sim.q4 >= 10), analytic.from.4c = p.atleast.pbinom,
  simulated.exactly.10  = mean(sim.q4 == 10),  analytic.from.4b = dbinom(10, n.patients, p.sens))
```

The simulated proportion (about `r round(mean(sim.q4 >= 10), 3)` with
this seed) matches the analytic value
`r round(p.atleast.pbinom, 3)` to within simulation noise, and the
simulated exactly-10 frequency likewise matches 0.1032 from parts
(a)–(b). Three routes — formula, distribution functions, brute-force
simulation — give one answer, which is the point of the whole of
Part A.

## 4(e) Using `qbinom()`: the smallest $k$ with $P(X \ge k) \le 0.05$

`qbinom()` inverts the CDF: `qbinom(0.95, n, p)` returns the smallest
count $q$ with $P(X \le q) \ge 0.95$, i.e. the count that already
covers 95% of the distribution. The event $X \ge k$ has probability
$\le 0.05$ exactly when $X \le k-1$ covers *at least* 95%, so the $k$
asked for is one more than that quantile. The chunk computes it that
way and then verifies every candidate $k$ directly with `pbinom()`
(`sapply()` over the candidates, as in Week2 Script.R, Part 2,
Code Chunk 13):

```{r q4e-qbinom}
# The 95% quantile of the distribution: P(X <= 14) is the first
# cumulative probability to reach 0.95.
q.95 <- qbinom(0.95, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)
q.95
pbinom(q.95, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)      # >= 0.95
pbinom(q.95 - 1, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)  # <  0.95

# Therefore the smallest k whose UPPER tail is at most 0.05 is:
k.star <- q.95 + 1
k.star

# Direct verification over all candidate thresholds k = 0..16:
# P(X >= k) = 1 - P(X <= k - 1), computed for each k with sapply().
tail.probs <- sapply(0:16, function(k) 1 - pbinom(k - 1, size = n.patients,
                                                  prob = p.sens))
data.frame(k = 0:16, P.X.at.least.k = round(tail.probs, 4))
min((0:16)[tail.probs <= 0.05])  # confirms k.star is the smallest such k
1 - pbinom(k.star - 1, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)      # P(X >= 15)
1 - pbinom(k.star - 2, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)      # P(X >= 14)
```

**Plain-English meaning.** $k = 15$. With a test of sensitivity 0.8
applied to 15 truly positive patients, "at least $k$ patients test
positive" only becomes a genuinely rare event — probability at most
5% — when $k$ is *all fifteen of them*: a perfect screen happens with
probability $0.8^{15} \approx 0.035$, while even "at least 14" is not
rare at all, at about 0.167 (it includes the fairly common
exactly-14 outcome). Note what this number is *not*: it is not a
typical value or a threshold we expect to stay above — the expected
count is 12, and counts of 14 or 15 are the distribution's *upper*
tail. $k = 15$ is the answer to "how many detections would have to pile
up before the pile-up itself would be surprising at the 5% level if
the sensitivity really were 0.8?" Because the binomial is discrete, no
threshold gives exactly 0.05: the achievable upper-tail probabilities
jump straight from 0.167 (at least 14) to 0.035 (all 15), and $k=15$ is
the first jump that lands at or below 0.05.

---

# Summary of Part A

* **Q1.** An estimator is a random variable; its denominator controls a
  bias–precision trade-off that is large at small $n$ and vanishes as
  $n$ grows. $n-1$ is aimed best, $n$ is biased low, $n-2$ is biased
  high, least steady, and undefined at $n = 2$.
* **Q2.** Under a true null, t-test p-values are uniform, brute-force
  rank p-values agree with them, and the agreement tightens as $n$
  grows because the t-test's variance estimate stabilises — the
  brute-force logic needs no such estimate and is the version that
  transfers to real data.
* **Q3.** The t-test tests *means* only. Two processes with the same
  mean but completely different shapes and spreads return textbook
  null behaviour — flat p-values, ~5% "significant" — so a
  non-significant t-test never means "the distributions are the same".
* **Q4.** The binomial family (`dbinom`/`pbinom`/`qbinom`/`rbinom`)
  answers counting questions exactly, and simulation with `rbinom()`
  reproduces those answers: $P(X = 10) \approx 0.1032$,
  $P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.9389$, and the smallest upper-tail threshold
  at the 5% level is $k = 15$.

---
